Question

How viable are ground supply corridors and potential staging areas across the lowland floodplain between Napier and Hastings (Hawke’s Bay, centered at 39.58°S, 176.88°E) following the February 14, 2023 peak of Cyclone Gabrielle, given observed radar inundation, infrastructure severances, and mapped building exposures?

The geographic coordinate center places this AOI squarely across the lower Heretaunga Plains, encompassing the confluence of the Tutaekuri, Ngaruroro, and Karamu systems around Pakowhai, Waiohiki, and Awatoto. Ground-truth radar evidence acquired at 07:07 UTC on February 14 shows massive backscatter attenuation in VV and total water index (WI = VV + VH), corresponding to an unsupervised two-dimensional Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) flood footprint of 12.52 km² (12.54% of the 99.87 km² AOI). The flood funnel shows clean convergence: starting from an unconstrained GMM component 1 detection of 13.08 km² (corroborated by k-means at 12.90 km²), surface water drops to 12.76 km² once permanent hydrography (JRC, WorldCover 80) is removed, and stabilizes at 12.52 km² after FABDEM bare-earth slope masking (≤10°) and minimal mapping unit (MMU) spatial filtering eliminate ~0.24 km² of slope and radar-noise artifacts.

The spatial distribution of this inundation reveals profound logistical isolation rather than widespread residential structural destruction within the mapped bounds. Out of 7,313 OpenStreetMap building outlines identified in the AOI, exactly 0 intersect the final radar flood mask. The third panel confirms that the main built-up agglomerations—suburban Taradale to the northwest, Hastings outskirts to the southwest, and Awatoto coastal fringe—sit topographically peripheral to the active river corridor. Only 0.035 km² of urban land cover was inundated. However, interpreting "0 buildings affected" as a lack of disaster impact would be a lethal mistake for relief dispatch: the entire central agricultural basin of Pakowhai was drowned, severing the vital transport links that connect Napier, Hastings, and the coastal logistics nodes.

Network analysis illustrates acute structural severance. While only 5.93 km (1.59%) of the 372.67 km road network within the AOI is inundated, this exposure concentrates across 24 critical ground edges spanning 10 distinct named roads. Foremost among these is the Hawke’s Bay Expressway (State Highway 2), alongside Brookfields Road, Gilbertson Road, Chesterhope Road, and Pakowhai-area connectors (Morley, Gilligan, Jessep, McLeod, Sissons, and Waitangi Roads). Most critically, 7 of these 10 flood-affected roads possess no alternate ground detour within the AOI, creating complete dead-end traps for rural orchards and peripheral lifestyle holdings. Only 3 affected roads offer in-AOI bypass routes. Because the Hawke’s Bay Expressway and Brookfields Road cross the drowned river berms, direct ground transit between Hastings and Napier through this corridor is completely compromised. Logistics planners cannot use the central arterial grid to stage relief supplies, nor can staging rely on local road bridges across the Tutaekuri or Ngaruroro rivers, 42 of which were tagged as bridge/tunnel infrastructure in OSM and excluded from surface edge checks (masking potential bridge approach washouts).

Several technical sensor limitations must qualify these conclusions: Sentinel-1 C-band (~10 m) specular reflectance detects standing open water, but double-bounce backscatter against standing trees, dense orchard canopies, and building walls can falsely brighten inundated rural homesteads, masking floodwaters directly surrounding structures. Furthermore, the 42 skipped bridge and tunnel edges mean that catastrophic structural washouts at river crossings (a hallmark of Cyclone Gabrielle) are not captured by two-dimensional surface intersection alone. Relief convoys arriving from coastal or southern axes must divert via peripheral western hill tracks or unflooded southern approaches (e.g., Karamu Road North, Te Ara Kahikatea) rather than venturing into the Pakowhai basin.
